description: KILLA is an educational Earth observation prototype from Esmeraldas. It uses NASA POWER historical data (2001–2025) to compare sample cells near Esmeraldas and Cuenca, explore temperature and precipitation trends, and question uncertainty. We welcome collaborators in Earth science, statistics, data visualization and web development. Working languages: Spanish and English. Current stage: working prototype.
summary: KILLA is a working educational Earth observation prototype for investigating environmental change with NASA data. Its professional dashboard combines a geographic sample map, annual time series, region comparison, date selection, trend estimates, nominal 95% confidence intervals and CSV export. The first implementation uses real NASA POWER MERRA-2 annual data for 2001–2025 from sample cells near Esmeraldas and Cuenca, Ecuador, covering 2-metre air temperature and corrected precipitation. KILLA addresses the challenge by showing what changed, where, by how much, and the assumptions behind uncertainty. Teachers and students can inspect the original observations, provenance and reproducible analysis. Global coverage and classroom co-design are future work; this prototype reports historical patterns rather than forecasts or causal attribution.
details: <h2>Purpose and impact</h2><p>KILLA turns historical Earth observations into an evidence laboratory for teachers and students. Starting in Ecuador, its long-term vision is a global educational observatory where people compare environmental change and question the strength and limits of conclusions. The current working prototype responds to Be An Earth System Trend Detective! with data selection, visualization and statistical trend analysis.</p><h2>Working prototype</h2><p>The interface lets a user select air temperature or precipitation, choose a sample near Esmeraldas or Cuenca, compare the second location, select a period of at least ten annual observations, display or hide a linear trend and download the selected values as CSV. The dashboard includes a geographic reference map, evidence summaries, annual time series, source records and a seven-slide English demonstration. The source code and reproducibility materials accompany the project.</p><h2>NASA data actually used</h2><p>We downloaded NASA POWER Monthly and Annual API responses for 2001–2025 at public query points near Esmeraldas (0.96, -79.65) and Cuenca (-2.90, -79.00). Response headers identify MERRA2 and API v2.10.0. We use the 25 annual YYYY13 entries for each of two variables at each location. T2M is annual mean 2-metre air temperature in degrees Celsius. PRECTOTCORR is annual mean daily corrected precipitation in mm/day, not an annual rainfall total. Original response bodies, request URLs, retrieval timestamps and SHA-256 hashes are available in the project provenance.</p><h2>Method and uncertainty</h2><p>Ordinary least squares fits each selected annual series against year. Slopes are reported per decade. Nominal two-sided 95% slope intervals use Student-t critical values with n-2 degrees of freedom. The implementation was tested against exact linear, constant, noisy reference and tabulated Student-t examples; the four full-period results were independently recomputed. The interface preserves yearly variation rather than displaying only the fitted line.</p><p>These classical intervals assume independent, constant-variance errors and an adequate linear mean. Those assumptions have not been established for these climate records. Temporal autocorrelation, model uncertainty and multiple comparisons are not corrected; no p-values or robust-detection labels are presented. A selected 25-year window is not a complete long-term climatology, and trend estimates do not establish causes or forecast future weather.</p><h2>Spatial meaning</h2><p>POWER meteorological estimates are based on MERRA-2 reanalysis, not a local station record or direct satellite image measurement. The native grid is 0.5 degrees latitude by 0.625 degrees longitude, roughly 56 by 70 km near the equator. The two query points select coarse sample cells; they are not city or province averages. Markers do not depict exact cell boundaries. Coastal mixing and terrain can affect representativeness.</p><h2>Tools, design and attribution</h2><p>The prototype uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with dependency-free statistical analysis and Node.js scripts for reproducibility. Leaflet renders the reference map with credited OpenStreetMap tiles; public-domain Natural Earth geography provides a separate fallback. The user-provided Rioverde dashboard informed the institutional interface structure. No municipal branding, private records or NASA logo assets were reused. OpenAI Codex assisted initial ideation, research, coding, analysis implementation, visual design, English writing and the presentation; the assistance and all external resources are disclosed.</p><h2>Next steps</h2><p>The current deliverable is a first working educational prototype. Classroom usability studies, more regions and variables, autocorrelation-aware analysis and broader geographic coverage remain future work. It is not an operational warning system or a validated planning service.</p>
